Churches, Cemeteries & John Paul II

St Mary Draperis

In 1909 Turks and Poles prayed here together for the Polish volunteers who fell in the Crimean War – even the future last caliph came to the Mass.

Theme
Churches, Cemeteries & John Paul II
District
Beyoğlu
Period
1909
Visiting
Open to visitors

The story

In summer 1909 a procession set out from this church such as, the Polish press said, Istanbul had never seen: Turks and Poles, carrying the flags of both nations, walking together to the house where Mickiewicz died.

St Mary Draperis is one of the oldest Catholic parishes in the city. In 1584 the Franciscans moved to Galata, where a Levantine woman, Clara Maria Draperis, gave them a house with a chapel and a wooden icon of the Virgin. In 1678 they built a church in Pera; it burned and fell several times, but the icon was always saved, and it still adorns the high altar. The church lies below street level, reached by steep steps.

After the Young Turk revolution of 1908, the Committee of Union and Progress, prompted by Tadeusz Gasztowtt – a Pole known in Istanbul as Seyfeddin – decided to honour the Polish volunteers who had died on the Ottoman side in the Crimean War, and Mickiewicz himself. According to the Polish émigré press, many Muslims, an imam among them, attended the Mass at St Mary Draperis. The guests included Committee leaders, Crimean War veterans, Prince Abdülmecid Efendi – later the last caliph – and a delegation from Adampol.

Then a procession with Polish and Ottoman banners went to Mickiewicz's house. A plaque was unveiled to 'the poet and great Polish patriot Adam Mickiewicz, friend of the Turks' (it has not survived), Selahaddin Bey spoke for the Committee, a sheep was sacrificed and portraits of the poet were handed out. Sources disagree on the date: the plaque bore 10 July 1909, a recent study gives 17 August. The Polish press wrote that no one had seen such a celebration for Poland since the partitions – at a time when Poland was not on the map.

How to visit

Enter from İstiklal Caddesi (No. 215) through the gateway with a statue of the Virgin in a niche, then down the steep steps to the church. It is run by Franciscan friars and Masses are mainly in Italian – check the current times on the board at the entrance. The Mickiewicz Museum is about 1 km away: walk up İstiklal towards Taksim, then turn west across Tarlabaşı Boulevard. The exact route of the 1909 procession is not known.
